strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical importance: explicitly addressing object-effect removal (shadows, reflections) that existing methods struggle with

Valuable dataset contribution (OBER): hybrid camera-captured and simulated data with 12,715 training samples, rich annotations (object masks, object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds), multi-object scenarios, and two complementary benchmarks

Comprehensive experimental validation: evaluation on three independent datasets (RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild), multiple metrics (PSNR, PSNR-BG, LPIPS, CLIP, ReMOVE), 8 baseline comparisons, and 30-participant user study showing strong preference (90.29% vs PowerPaint, 84.69% vs RORem)
Strong empirical results with particularly impressive background preservation (PSNR-BG: 35.14 vs. RORem's 27.95 on OBER-Test) and convincing qualitative improvements across diverse scenarios
Thorough ablation studies (Table 2) clearly demonstrating the contribution of each component: mask loss, simulated data, and attention-guided fusion

Technically sound approach: input design using original image is well-motivated; object-effect attention logically decouples foreground removal from background reconstruction; attention-guided fusion effectively leverages learned representations

Good reproducibility: detailed implementation details (resolution, batch size, iterations, learning rate), hyperparameters (guidance scale, denoising steps), and uses public base model (SDXL-Inpainting)
Robustness demonstrated: handles coarse user-drawn masks, extends to object insertion/movement applications, qualitatively handles complex multi-object occlusion scenarios
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Object-Effect Attention is a straightforward application of existing cross-attention supervision techniques (following [16, 35, 23]); Attention-Guided Fusion is conventional soft masking/blending. Core contribution is engineering-focused rather than introducing new concepts.

Dataset concerns despite improvements: only 2,715 camera-captured pairs (relatively small for deep learning); reflection pair simulation is ad-hoc with only 50 manually curated pairs; simulated data uses straightforward alpha blending without addressing complex lighting/material properties; fixed 512×512 resolution limits modern applications

Significant experimental bias: OBER is used for both training and testing, inflating apparent improvements. RORD-Val results are more modest (21.61→26.40 PSNR vs. 26.4→32.98 on OBER-Test). Small test sets (OBER-Test: 160 samples, RORD-Val: 343 after deduplication) limit statistical significance.

Critical technical details missing or underspecified: threshold value for effect mask computation not provided; Gaussian blur kernel size for attention map smoothing not specified; object-aware dilation/erosion strategy lacks detail; no sensitivity analysis for these hyperparameters

Significant acknowledged limitations severely impact real-world applicability: method struggles with multiple overlapping shadows (cannot disentangle); fails on extremely large/long shadow regions with residual artifacts. These are common scenarios that restrict practical deployment.

Limited novelty in comparison with closest baseline: improvements over RORem [15] (the only method specifically designed for object-effect removal) are less dramatic than over general inpainting methods, suggesting dataset specialization rather than methodological advances

Incomplete generalization analysis: only evaluated with SDXL-Inpainting; no cross-dataset training/testing; no evaluation on other diffusion models; unclear how well approach transfers to different architectures or domains
Missing computational analysis: no inference time, memory requirements, or model size comparisons provided. No analysis of why/when attention maps help beyond visualization

Unjustified design choices: eight shadow direction categories lack justification; alpha map formula (Eq. 1) appears ad-hoc without theoretical grounding; multi-object simulation limited to same lighting direction restricts diversity

Incomplete related work comparison: recent methods OmniPaint [39] and LayerDecomp [36] mentioned but not experimentally compared; limited discussion of differences with RORem; ObjectDrop comparison limited due to unavailable dataset

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitation: existing methods fail to remove object-associated visual effects (shadows, reflections)

strengths: Well-motivated problem: The paper clearly identifies and addresses a genuine limitation in existing object removal methods—failure to remove associated visual effects like shadows and reflections.

Substantial dataset contribution: OBER provides 12,715 carefully curated samples with rich annotations (object masks, object-effect masks, RGBA foregrounds, multi-object scenarios), promised for public release.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multi-benchmark validation (RORD-Val, OBER-Test, OBER-Wild), multiple metrics, extensive baseline comparisons, user study, and ablation studies demonstrate thorough evaluation.
Strong empirical results: Achieves state-of-the-art across multiple benchmarks with particularly strong performance on background preservation (PSNR-BG: 35.62 vs. 30.04 for second-best).
Clear technical soundness: Method design is correct and well-motivated, including proper cross-attention guidance, reasonable mask loss formulation, and valid alpha-blending strategy.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in method components: ATA is standard cross-attention guidance with simple mask loss (Eq. 2 is just mean difference), AGF is straightforward alpha-blending, and SVDS is an engineering heuristic. Components lack technical depth and sophistication.

Incomplete fairness of comparisons: ObjectClear is trained with explicit object-effect mask supervision (M_fg), a form of privileged information not available to baselines during training. While Table 7 partially addresses this, much of the improvement conflates better training data annotation with algorithmic innovation.

Modest per-component gains: Table 2 shows ATA contributes only ~0.27 dB PSNR (27.29→27.56); most gains come from AGF (0.0805→0.0348 LPIPS), which is primarily a post-processing fusion heuristic, not core algorithmic innovation.
Significant acknowledged limitations: Section 8.9 admits failure on overlapping shadows from multiple objects—a realistic scenario. No analysis of real-world prevalence of these failure cases.

Dataset-specific evaluation: OBER-Wild lacks ground truth and uses modified ReMOVE† metric without sufficient justification. Resolution limited to 512×512. No evaluation on varying resolutions or systematic analysis by object/effect type.
Missing fair-comparison analysis: No experiment training baseline methods with object-effect mask supervision to isolate method contribution from data quality contribution.
Presentation clarity: Distinction between dataset contribution vs. method contribution could be clearer upfront. Difference maps with heatmaps are difficult to parse. Paper is somewhat verbose.

Fair comparison methodology addressing mask input conditions (Section 8.3, Table 7) showing ObjectClear's advantage persists even when baselines use ground-truth effect masks
